items.title: Queue is growing, not just deep
items.explanation: The waiting queue grew by 41.7 requests across the last 1m0s and now stands at 62. Unlike a deep but stable queue, this does not reach equilibrium on its own: queueing delay will keep rising for as long as the trend holds.
items.suggested_action: Treat as a capacity shortfall and shed or scale now rather than waiting for a latency alert. Check the companion findings for this workload to see whether the bottleneck is compute, KV cache, or admission.

items.title: Requests queueing while the GPU is saturated
items.explanation: 62 requests have been waiting with the GPU above 80% utilisation for 1m0s. The accelerator is doing useful work and still cannot keep up, so raising concurrency on this replica will lengthen the queue rather than drain it.
items.suggested_action: Add replicas, or reduce the work per request — a smaller or quantised model, or shorter generations. Check whether an autoscaler is already trying and blocked (see IFA-SCL-001 and IFA-SCL-002).

items.title: GPU memory near capacity
items.explanation: GPU memory has been above 90% for 1m0s, currently 92.9%. For a workload with a preallocated KV cache this is often by design — check whether the number moves at all before treating it as a leak.
items.suggested_action: If the figure is static it is the runtime's own reservation and is expected. If it climbs, look for another process sharing the device, or a growing set of loaded adapters or models.

items.title: Time to first token dominated by queueing
items.explanation: p95 TTFT is 903ms against a 500ms target, and about 87% of it (788ms) is queue time before the scheduler admits the request. Prefill accounts for roughly the remaining 115ms, so tuning prompt handling would barely move the number a user sees.
items.suggested_action: Add serving capacity, or admit requests sooner by raising the concurrency limit if the GPU has headroom. Routing long prompts to a separate pool also helps, because they are what holds admission slots open.
